summary: A draft design from SRI-ARC for a protocol covering both text and graphics, put together from existing ideas rather than new ones. The authors were concerned that the graphics protocol suggested in RFC 493 handled text poorly and would shape future graphics interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 553 proposes a way for a network application to manage both text and graphics on a remote display. It describes two ways to organize display content, while leaving the full command encoding for later work.

subtitle: A draft design for sending text and graphics through a TELNET connection.

tldr.problem: The authors wanted a graphics protocol that could also handle text and support a range of display devices and applications.
tldr.mechanism: The draft proposes two display-file styles, segmented and structured, with text and graphics commands carried within TELNET connections.
tldr.outcome: The document describes a draft architecture and commands, but postpones the actual encoding until after further discussion.

sections.title: A Shared Model for Text and Graphics
sections.content:
The authors are concerned that the graphics proposal in RFC 493 handles text poorly and operates at too low a level for a wide range of devices. They propose two display-file levels: segmented and structured. Applications can use simple display elements or a structure with reusable display components.

The draft treats an application as controlling a remote display file. It proposes carrying graphics commands in TELNET, marked by begin- and end-graphics command characters or by TELNET's 8-bit transparent mode. It also expects ordinary, unescorted characters to reach the terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: The draft aims to let one network connection carry typed text and graphics commands. It offers a simple display style and a more organized style for applications that need reusable elements.

sections.title: Segmented and Structured Displays
sections.content:
A segmented display file contains named segments made from primitive display units, such as strings, dots or lines. The available operations add, delete or replace segments, and changes update the display automatically.

A structured display file contains named subpictures made from primitive units and call units. A call unit refers to another subpicture and can apply transformations such as translation, scaling or rotation. This structure allows one subpicture to be reused within another. The draft also defines text-oriented TTY units so a display can handle terminal-like input and output.
sections.plainLanguage: Segments are named groups of display elements that can be changed directly. Structured files can also reuse one named picture inside another, with changes such as moving or scaling it.

sections.title: Editing and Interacting with a Display
sections.content:
The draft lists commands to request a display file, create and remove segments or subpictures, add strings, lines and dots, control visibility, and reset display state. Structured files can be updated on the screen after edits. The draft also proposes optional direct-feedback features such as dragging, tracking, inking and rubber banding, with commands to check and control support.

Input may include keyboard characters, binary-device events and cursor coordinates. The application can query the terminal environment and display state, including screen size, devices, cursor position and supported commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can create or change display elements and ask what the terminal supports. The proposal also describes optional ways for a display to respond directly to cursor movement.

sections.title: Encoding Was Still to Come
sections.content:
The draft gives encoding principles: commands are framed by begin- and end-graphics markers, numbers use groups of significant bits, and subpicture and unit names are 14-bit numbers. It notes that characters above the basic set were not standardized.

The actual encoding was deferred because the authors expected the design to change after a Network Graphics Group meeting. The document therefore provides a draft design and command descriptions, not a complete encoding specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors outline how commands and names might be represented, but do not finish the full encoding. They planned to revisit it after further discussion.
